content: An embryo is a multicellular diploid eukaryotic organism in its earliest stage of development. The term embryo originates from the Greek word meaning that which grows. In humans, the organism is referred to as an embryo from the moment of fertilization until the end of the eighth week of development. After this period, it is called a fetus. The process of embryo development is known as embryogenesis. In sexually reproducing organisms, fertilization occurs when a sperm cell fuses with an egg cell, forming a zygote. This zygote contains the complete genetic material of both parents, with 50% of its DNA derived from each. In plants, animals, and some protists, the zygote undergoes mitotic cell division, resulting in a multicellular organism, which is the embryo. In animals, the zygote develops into an embryo through distinct stages, including the blastula, gastrula, and organogenesis. The blastula stage is characterized by a fluid-filled cavity called the blastocoel, surrounded by a layer of cells known as blastomeres. During gastrulation, the cells of the blastula undergo organized processes of division, migration, and invasion, forming two (diploblastic) or three (triploblastic) germ layers. In triploblastic organisms, these layers are the ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The arrangement and positioning of these layers vary significantly between species. In vertebrates, a unique group of embryonic cells called the neural crest is sometimes referred to as a fourth germ layer and is thought to have played a critical role in the evolution of head structures. During organogenesis, interactions between the germ layers, along with the cells' ability to respond to developmental signals, lead to the differentiation of organ-specific cell types. For instance, in neurogenesis, a subset of ectodermal cells is designated to form the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Modern developmental biology investigates the molecular mechanisms underlying various types of organogenesis, such as angiogenesis (formation of blood vessels), chondrogenesis (formation of cartilage), myogenesis (formation of muscle), and osteogenesis (formation of bone). A general principle in embryology is that structures that evolved earlier in evolutionary history tend to develop earlier in the embryo. For example, the backbone, a shared feature of all vertebrates, is one of the first structures to form in vertebrate embryos. In contrast, the human cerebrum, the most advanced part of the brain, develops later in the process. In plants, the embryo is a component of the seed and consists of precursor tissues for the leaves, stem, and root, as well as one or more cotyledons. When the embryo begins to grow out of the seed, it is referred to as a seedling. Non-seed-producing plants, such as bryophytes and ferns, also produce embryos. In these plants, the embryo is a young organism that remains attached to the parental gametophyte. In placental mammals, the embryo is defined as the organism from the first division of the zygote until it transitions into the fetal stage. In humans, this period extends from implantation in the uterus to the end of the eighth week of development. After this point, the organism is referred to as a fetus until birth. Human Embryo Development Weeks 1-3: Approximately 5-7 days after fertilization, the blastula attaches to the uterine wall (endometrium) in a process called implantation. During this time, connections between the mother and the embryo begin to form, including the development of the umbilical cord. The embryo's growth is organized around an axis that will later develop into the spine and spinal cord. The brain, spinal cord, heart, and gastrointestinal tract begin to form. Weeks 4-5: The embryo produces chemical signals that halt the mother's menstrual cycle. Neurogenesis begins, and brain activity can be detected by the sixth week. The heart starts to beat, and limb buds appear, marking the initial stages of arm and leg development. Organogenesis, the formation of organs, is underway. At this stage, the head constitutes about half of the embryo's axial length and more than half of its mass. The brain develops into five distinct regions, and the vertebrae and bones begin to form. Blood circulation also starts. Weeks 6-8: By this time, myogenesis (muscle formation) and neurogenesis have progressed to the point where the embryo can move. The eyes begin to form, and organogenesis continues. Hair starts to develop, and all essential organs are present. Facial features begin to take shape. By the end of the eighth week, the embryonic stage concludes, and the fetal stage begins. Ethical Considerations of the Human Embryo The status of the human embryo is a topic of debate among bioethicists. Some Christian ethicists argue that an embryo possesses personhood from the moment of conception. For example, Gilbert Meileander, a professor of Christian ethics, asserts that a new individual human being comes into existence at conception because the zygote's genotype is established at this point. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) defines the embryonic stage as the beginning of the development of the human form.
